utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, you can call the case, thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case number IT-99-36-T --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case number IT-99-36-T, the Prosecutor versus Radoslav Brdjanin and Momir Talic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Brdjanin, good afternoon to you. Can you hear me in a language that you can understand? THE ACCUSED BRDJANIN: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. I can hear you and understand you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. And you may sit down. General Talic, can you hear me in a language that you can understand? THE ACCUSED TALIC: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. I can hear you in a language I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you too. You may sit down. Thank you. Appearance for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Joanna Korner and Denise Gustin, case manager. Good afternoon, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Appearances for Mr. Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. I'm John Ackerman and Marela Jevtovic for Mr. Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you too. Appearances for General Talic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Slobodan Zecevic and Natasha Ivanovic-Fauveau for General Talic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you too. Any preliminaries?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Only as regards the Rule 92 order that Your Honours issued. It is our intention to call all four witnesses for cross-examination, as Your Honours ordered, limited in the way that Your Honours, ordered to half an hour per defendant, accused. And we will call them, all four, within two days at the end of the Kljuc evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Subject to -- I should add they haven't been contacted yet to be told that's what's going to have to happen. So subject to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I thank you. So usher, please bring in the witness. Thank you. Do you think you will conclude with the witness today?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I propose to conclude, whatever happens, before the first break. I think Mr. Filipovic has had enough of me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can I ask you to repeat your solemn declaration once more, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. And you may sit down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And Ms. Korner will proceed and conclude with her examination-in-chief. Ms. Korner. Examined by Ms. Korner: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Filipovic, I want to pick up the story where you left off yesterday. You told us how you were beaten outside the police station and that you were then taken inside the police station. What happened to you when you were inside the police station?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They didn't take me inside because if they had taken me inside, I would have gone in on any own two feet. They carried me inside in an unconscious condition. I came to in the office of the interrogator Todo Gajic. From then on, that is, when -- from when I came -- regained consciousness until half past 5.00 on that same day, as far as I was able to count and recollect, I lost consciousness seven to eight times. They beat me, but the interrogator Todo Gajic himself never beat me because he knew me personally. And in his presence I was not beaten. But he first asked me, "Muhis, where is Omer?" And I said, "Omer has gone to Krasulje together with Vinko to secure Duca's body being taken out." And he said to me, "I told you not to engage in politics. You're a got professional. It would have been better for you not to get involved in politics." That is the only thing that the interrogator Todo Gajic would say to me. Then he would get up and walk out and then people who I didn't know who were not from Kljuc came in wearing the uniforms of the Serbian police, camouflage blue uniforms. They would beat me up. And when they left, then Todo Gajic would come back in. I think it -- on the third occasion they ordered me to strip, and all I had on me was my slip. They took everything else off. And then they beat me on my naked body with truncheons, their boots. I think it was the fifth time. One of them - I don't know his name - but I know that he used to drive a van in Sumarstvo in Kljuc. His nickname was Lizija. And he would put a knife to my neck. And as I was lying in the middle of the office helpless, he would roll a grenade on the floor. And if it had -- as if it had remote control, it rolled right up to me. And then he said, "Look at the Ustasha. He even has a hand grenade," whereas I only had my underwear on. I managed to pluck up so much strength to say, "I never saw any such bombs like that one," because when I served in the military, I never saw such a hand grenade. This was of a newer brand. Then he put the grenade in my mouth and said, "Shall I activate it?" And I begged God that he did that, because if one Muhamed got killed, five Chetniks would get killed as well. So I prayed to God that he activate the bomb regardless; however, I knew he wouldn't do that, because the Serbian soldiers are great cowards. They are afraid for their own lives. This was proven at the very end of the war when we formed our own real army. And sometime around 5.00 p.m. a man walked into the office. I can't recollect his name. He was a police commander. I'll remember his name later. And he attacked them when he saw the condition I was in.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you pause there for a moment, please. First of all, when the interrogator, Gajic, came back in, was he questioning you each time about your brother?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only that one time, the first time. And then when he came in, sometimes it was Gajic; on one occasion it was Zoran Vracar, a butcher. He was also in the reserve force. And a couple of other men I knew would come in, and they always asked the same question: "Muhamed, what was all this for? You're now against us. Wasn't it fine when we were together?" And I said, "I don't know who is rebelling. We were always in favour of co-existence with you." However, I can state here that not a single inhabitant of Kljuc hit me except for this one who put a grenade and a knife to my body, but even he is not really from Kljuc. He's from Donji Ribnik. And when the police commander came, he yelled at them and swore at them and said all kinds of things like "Are you beasts or policemen? How are you treating the man?" So I don't know whether that was what he really thought or whether he was trying to impress me, but he said, "Take the man to the cell." And I was then taken about 5.00 p.m. to the cell. And when I saw all the people inside, it became clear to me that it had nothing to do with what they called a rebellion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before we deal with the people in the cell, can I ask you this: You told us that the police commander, seeing the state you were in, told them to stop. At that stage, at the end of all these beatings, what sort of injuries did you have?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, let me say I just remembered the name of the police commander. It's Dragan Stojicic. As for the injuries, I couldn't see myself. My body was still warm. I was covered in blood. And when they took me in, I was still in my underwear. Then they gave me my clothes, and I quickly had to put them on on the way to the cell, and the cell is in the basement, dark.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And my body was still warm. It was only on the third day that I felt the consequences of those beatings, when I cooled off, and I realised that I couldn't move. I couldn't walk.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's what I was going to ask you. I'm going to come on to the injuries to your leg, but was it at that stage that you received the injuries to your legs?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume it was then because apart from that time when I was beaten in the police station, I was also beaten in front of the police station when they took us out at 6.00 and then in front of the truck when we were being loaded and then seven or eight times from Kljuc to Mali Logor (redacted), so that I must have been injured in that period of time. In the cell I recognised Rebac Domagoj, a Croat; Darko Dzaja, a Croat; Leopold Flat, a German dentist; Branko Dzaja, Darko's father, a Croat; Luka Brkic, a Croat; and several other Muslims. And then I realised that they had nothing to do with what they were accusing us of, because I was thinking to myself, They said that we were rebelling, whereas these Croats and this German, Dr. Flat, had absolutely nothing to do with the Muslims, so that it became clear to me that this was all intended to cleanse Kljuc of non-Serbs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, the people that you saw in the cell with you, you said one was a German and others were Croats. What sort of position did they hold in Kljuc?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were also some Muslims. Well, let me tell you. Leopold Flat is a dentist. Luka Brkic, a sales clerk in the forestry company. Rebac Domagoj, a teacher of art. Branko Dzaja, a veterinary surgeon, a vet. His son, Danko, was a student. He hadn't graduated, so he worked as a taxi driver in town. They were all well off, employed; the Muslims also. There was Mirsad Sehic among the Muslims; Djelic Mehmed; myself. There were 21 of us. And Kujundzic - I can't remember his first name - he was a driver. He was unconscious, whereas all the rest of us were able to communicate amongst ourselves with our eyes. We didn't dare talk, because the Serbs would be peeping through the hole in the door. And if we talked, they would curse us, our balija mothers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. You've already told us that at around half past 5.00 to 6.00 you were taken out of the cell. And when you were taken out, it was at that stage that you were thrown down the steps of the police station. You were Placed onto a truck and kept in Mali Logor. How long were you kept in Mali Logor?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, when they took us, there was another round of beating. There were steps for us to climb up to board the truck. And our hands were tied so tightly behind our backs that for four months I couldn't move my fingers. And climbing onto the truck, I fell. I couldn't climb, because it is very difficult to climb if you don't have your hands to help you up. And as I fell, all of them kicked me, and a policeman, Jovo Perisic came up and said, "What are you doing to the man?" And he said, "He's the main Turk. Leave him be and board him onto the truck." And then they picked me up like a bag of cement, by the shoulders and the legs, and threw me onto the truck. When they drove us from Kljuc to Banja Luka, the truck stopped for the first time. I think it was around 7.00 p.m. when the truck stopped near Hasljnak [phoen]. There was an inhabited locality. And a Chetnik came out and said, "You, leader, come here." And then somebody says, "There are no leaders," he said. And he said, "Yes, there is. Filipovic is amongst you. Let him come." And I somehow came up to him. And as I approached, the Serbs are cowards. Though we were all tied -- tied up, he didn't dare climb up onto the truck. But from the road he hit me twice with his fist in the chin and I fainted. He yelled that I should get up again, and I didn't want to, so I thought to myself, He wouldn't dare climb up. So this went for seven or eight times until we reached the Mali Logor barracks. In the meantime, Mrsic Enes managed somehow to untie his hands, and he untied the hands of all of us, and we all tied our hands in front because after all it's easier to defend yourself when you have your hands tied in front. And when they wanted to beat me again, I would protect myself. So when we arrived at the Mali Logor, I kept praying to God to save me or to help me die. And then they shouted out, "Give us Mehmed Begic," who disclosed the codes in the post office, and he's a graduate electrical engineer working in the post office. They first took me and threw me down and all the others on top. I was choking from the weight, but I thought to myself, There is God after all, because he has saved me from the beatings. And I was choking. But all the beatings were focussed on Mehmed Begic in Mali Logor. He had a good leather jacket. But from the blows, the jacket was torn to pieces. In the meantime, maybe after an hour of beating, Zoran came up. We recognised him. I recognised him too. We called him Brkin. His father was a Brko, a mustachio [phoen]. He was a policeman in the former Yugoslavia in the reserve force, and he retired as a policeman. He pretended in front of us, and he cursed God and he said, "What are you doing? These are my people from Kljuc. They're fine people." My colleague, Medo Fadil he said, "A colleague, this neighbour of ours, will save us." And I said, "Excuse me. Fuck you. No one is going to save us." And then Brkin to impress us yelled at them for a while, and they stopped. But they had carried out what they intended to do. They had beaten up Begic Mehmed. Then they boarded us onto the truck again and drove us to Stara Gradiska. And I wish to point out there was a hole on the tarpaulin on the truck and a man nicknamed Kuljo would peep through. And he would say, "We've passed this spot and that spot," and he kept saying, "So long as they don't take us to Kula, because that is where they kill people." So he told us that we had passed Kula, and we realised we had come to Bosanska Gradiska. We wondered where they would take us. And I said then, "We are going to Stara Gradiska," which was a well-known prison in the former Yugoslavia. So I thought, That is where they would take us, because Stara Gradiska is just across the river and it is situated in the Republic of Croatia. And when they took us inside to the prison, inside the prison in Stara Gradiska – (redacted).

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Pages 9597 to 9599 – decision to redact -order dated on 2 April 2003.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The next day a doctor came, a lady, to examine us. And when she saw -- so this was my second day in cell number 3. And the doctor required that we get up, and I said, "Madam doctor, I can't get up. Even when I do, it's with great effort." (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't move, so the guard designated Teufik to carry me to the ambulance, to the clinic. And as he carried me, the worst thing is one cannot see oneself. And Teufik asked me, "What do I look like?" And this Chetnik going in front of us says, "Don't talk," he yelled at us. And I whispered into his ear, "You're swollen. You're blue." And he said -- he probably was able to see himself, so he said, "Believe me. I may look awful, but you're a hundred times worse." So when I entered into the doctor's surgery, I saw above the sink that there was a mirror, and I asked the doctor, "Could I wash my face?" And she said, "Yes, please do. You've come to see a doctor. You're not in prison now." So I went to wash, and as I was washing I looked at the mirror, and the Chetnik escorting me, he wouldn't let me look. But the doctor chased him out of the surgery and said, "You have nothing to do here. This is a patient." And when he left, I washed well. I put my head under the tap. Believe it or not, my head had doubled in size. One couldn't see where my nose was, whether I had a nose or not. My head was like a football. And then she prescribed penicillin and said, "You should thank God that I still have some penicillin in reserve. And for as long as I'm here, you will be given penicillin." And true enough, every day I was given shots in the morning and in the evening, and the fifth or sixth day after that this lady doctor disappeared. Where she went, I don't know. Most probably she didn't suit the leadership, because she treated me nicely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you receive any treatment after she left?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I received penicillin. And since Stara Gradiska is near Bosanska Gradiska, I was told to get ready and I was taken to a van and I was taken to Bosanska Gradiska to the hospital, along with Asim Egrlic. But we were not allowed to talk amongst each other. We just looked at each other. We exchanged glances and from that we knew what was going on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you receive treatment at the hospital in Bosanska Gradiska?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will speak about that. When I reached Bosanska Gradiska, I was put in a corridor. I was on one of those carriages and Egrlic on another. The corridor was 20 or 30 metres long.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We waited for a surgeon for about half an hour. When the surgeon came out from an operation he was doing -- a gentleman came. He was a true gentleman. There were three nurses. One of them received me with a traditional Muslim welcome, Selamalaykum. I couldn't believe her, that she was a Muslim, so I didn't even want to respond. But she spoke this very fluently, like a true Muslim woman. But again, I didn't want to respond. And then this surgeon came. He examined me, and he told me, "Sir, Mr. Filipovic, you must go to a larger centre than our own. Your leg has to be operated on. We in Bosanska Gradiska are unable to perform such an operation." (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And for the first time in my life I heard the term "third countries." When I answered the doctor, I told him that I did not want to go to Banja Luka. And he asked me why. "Well, my surname does not bode well in Banja Luka. When they learn my name is Filipovic, I will be beaten even more severely than there in the prison." Then he said, "Mr. Filipovic, when you go to third countries, you ask to be operated on immediately. I can only help you in this way. He took a syringe. He called a nurse. He removed two syringes of fluid from my knee, and he said, "This is all I can do to alleviate your pain for the time being." He gave me a cast. He bandaged my whole leg. It was in a cast up to my ankle but only from the inside. From the outside, it was bandaged. When night fell, the pains would start.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Can we just pause then and deal with your leg. First of all, you say he extracted fluid from your knee. Was anything broken as far as you could tell?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was that? What part of the leg?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I didn't really know what was going on, and I didn't know until I came to London. Because without an x-ray -- and I didn't know what was wrong with me really.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. But clearly your leg, from what you say, was swollen because they had to extract water from your knee.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Other than that visit to the hospital in Bosanska Gradiska, until such time as you were transferred from Manjaca, were you taken to any other hospital?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You remained in Stara Gradiska, I think, until the 15th of June. During the time you were there --

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- how many people were in the cell with you?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have been listening for half an hour the evidence regarding Stara Gradiska. Stara Gradiska is in Croatia and it is not in the indictment. At one moment this camp was in the indictment. And we wanted to be expurged [as interpreted] from the indictment because it is a camp which is in another republic and Judge Hunt accepted this and he ordered the Prosecutor to amend the indictment, not to have Gradiska figure in the indictment. So I understand well that the witness wishes to tell us his whole experience but who the guards were in Stara Gradiska. That is something which is not relevant to this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Korner. I'm --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's quite -- I'm sorry, Your Honour. It's absolutely right. Stara Gradiska was in the indictment. It was removed because it was in Croatia. That, in our submission, is neither here nor there. It is part and parcel of the evidence in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: There I agree with you. Where I would like you to reply to Madam Fauveau is whether the question as to whether the police or the guards were military or -- is relevant or not, since we're talking of guards in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It matters no odds, Your Honour. Your Honour is going to hear evidence that this camp, this barracks, came under the command of the 5th Corps. There's an order -- it's already been read in evidence, I think, from General Talic, ordering the movement of troops. It's not part of the indictment because of Croatia. It's similar fact evidence, which is relevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It was already in Croatian territory at the time, no?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's always been in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's been in Croatia throughout. But the fact is that for whatever historical Yugoslav -- JNA reason, it came under the command of the 5th Corps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But the effective command.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The effective command of General Talic. There's an order. I think so we looked at it later on.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When we were making our exception and when Judge Hunt did made his determination that this should not be in the indictment, the Prosecutor did not react to this, respond to this. She should have done that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Your Honour, we say whether or not it's in the indictment is neither here nor there. This is a matter of similar fact, closely connected evidence. It's not part of the indictment because, as Judge Hunt ruled, it's in Croatia. We didn't appeal the ruling because we thought we had enough camps. But there is no conceivable way that we can ignore the evidence of what happened in Stara Gradiska.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What I want to know -- and perhaps I'll get an answer from you first before the witness may proceed -- is I take it - otherwise I would have stopped the series of questions - that the gentleman, the witness, was taken to Stara Gradiska by Serb guards and that he was --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- kept there under the surveillance of Serb guards.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Correct. And so irrespective of the question as to whether it's in or out of the indictment - and we agree that it is definitely out of the indictment - I'm going to allow the question or the Prosecution to proceed with this question because we're still talking of Serb guards and the Prosecution is alleging that those Serb guards -- you are alleging, and then it stands to be proved -- that those Serb guards or at least where the gentleman was taken and kept in Stara Gradiska fell under the control of the 5th Corps.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The 5th Corps did not exist at that particular moment, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That is ha contention of the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The 5th Corps as it was -- the 1st -- the 5th Corps of the JNA, the 1st Corps -- Krajina Corps as it became after the 28th, on or about this very period.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But the 1st Krajina Corps of Republika Srpska was never responsible in Stara Gradiska, and that is where the problem lies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That stands to be proved. I mean, that's something that the Prosecution needs to prove, Madam Fauveau. I mean, it's -- I know it's a contention by the Defence, and it's a contention that --

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is a different republic which had its own bodies and its own armed forces.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm -- I'm slightly distressed that the witness's account of what is clearly a harrowing event is being interrupted by an argument of law. I propose at this moment to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, please proceed. I mean, our decision --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please proceed. And without prejudice to the whole issue as to whether the 1st Krajina Corps was responsible for -- for Stara Gradiska and also -- because the witness hasn't even answered your question, first. He may as well answer us by telling us these guards had nothing to do with the army. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Filipovic, can you just deal with that. The guards --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please. She is putting the question again to you, Mr. Filipovic. And you are now kindly asked to answer it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Filipovic, were the guards policemen, ordinary policemen, or military, or a mixture of both?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am irritated by these interruptions of the Defence. As I as a prisoner was taken to -- as a prisoner to Stara Gradiska, why then wasn't the question raised? A citizen of Bosnia is taken to a different republic. I'm a citizen of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and Stara Gradiska is the Republic of Croatia. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. So --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He hasn't answered the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No. All right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Filipovic, I know it's irritating, but what we're trying to do is let you tell your story. So if you'll just concentrate on this.(redacted) Page 9609 – decision to redact -order dated on 2 April 2003.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, you say that your brother, Omer Filipovic, was brought into your cell. When did you first become aware that he, too, was at Stara Gradiska?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, no what? I thought you said he was brought to your cell.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. On June 11th, the first day of Bajram, my brother was taken to my cell. Subsequently he told me that the guard had taken him -- he said, "Brother, you have half an hour. You can talk together. But when the guard changes at 6.00, the -- you will have more time to talk." I didn't know what was going on. Omer was telling me that he was in a cell with a Serb, a good Serb from Derventa. And he is a rich Serb, and the guard is someone who supports him, and he made it possible for us -- for the two of us to meet, and we spent half an hour together, and then the guard said, "Finish now. And now we have to go back or else I'll be in trouble." Omer told me during that first hour, he told me all that had happened, how he wasn't able to recognise me. He told me about how he had heard that I was in Gradiska. We were vis-a-vis -- we were -- I was in the cell vis-a-vis his, and he told me that he had heard that my name called for syringes. I asked who -- which Filipovic was there, and he said Muhamed Filipovic. Well, that's not saying much because there are four by that name in Kljuc. I asked, "How does he look?" "He is bald, thin, and he wears a beard." And he said, "Well, no, that is not my brother. My brother is big." I used to be a big, sturdy person. And Omer then asked the guard, "Go and see in the book of records what the father's name is." And the guard came to Omer and he said, "Does the name Suljo mean anything," to me? Well, that is the name of my father. And he said, "Well, that is my brother." And when Omer saw me, he couldn't recognise me. I had been so dehydrated. When the guard said I was thin and bald, well, all that had happened in a period of ten days. I used to have 120 kilos, and all of a sudden I got thin. I never used to be bald. I got bald from all the stresses I experienced.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Can we deal now with the rest of this fairly shortly, and then I want to deal with Manjaca. Had your brother been beaten at all when you saw him?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. In Stara Gradiska he had not been beaten. He told me so. He said, "Brother, I am very sorry what happened to you." He said, "They are not beating me. Todo Gajic from Kljuc comes to me to question me on a daily basis." And he says, "Thanks to Vinko Kondic, I am still alive, because Vinko Kondic sticks to some rules. Now, if the others, Banjac were to be asked, I would not be alive today. Vinko sticks to the rules."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I want to talk, please, about Manjaca. And can I tell you, Mr. Filipovic, the Judges have heard a great deal of evidence already about it, so I'm just going to concentrate on certain aspects. Were you taken to Manjaca on the 15th of June?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was your brother Omer also taken there at the same time?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, when you arrived at Manjaca -- or before you arrived, were you beaten?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. They didn't beat us, but it is as if they had. The bus usually carries 50 people. There were 150 of us in the bus. The outside temperature was 30 degrees, and the driver put on the heating as if it were winter. And we were suffocating there. The driver opened the window next to him. He did this consciously so as to have a draft, but the rest of us were suffocating. I would have preferred to have been beaten by a truncheon than suffocate like that. We were one on top of the others.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you got to the camp, were you beaten at the camp?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that on the day of your arrival or later?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the day I arrived the guard -- I found out his name was Zeljko Bulatovic -- later on he asked, "Have these people had their names written down?" We didn't know why this was said. When you say that, it means you have to write down your name in the record book. But for them it meant were you beaten. They said, "No." And then Zeljko Bulatovic came up. He wrote my name in. In fact, he beat me up until I fell. Then when I was beaten up, my late brother came to me to try to help me up. Then Zeljko Bulatovic started beating my brother and said, "Why are you helping an Ustasha?" Omer put up his head and he said, "I have to do that. It is my brother." And he said, "Well, when you have to, then here are some beatings for you too." Then they started beating Omer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that the first time that your brother had been beaten, as far as you were aware?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These were the first beatings of my brother Omer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, during the course of your stay in Manjaca, were you interrogated?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, once.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And at the end of that interrogation, did you make a written statement?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The person interrogating me was writing things down and then I signed something. First I was taken there and then I was hit by a rifle butt. I could barely walk, and he kept hitting me to walk faster, so I was beaten a few times before I reached there, to the office where the investigator was, from the cattle shed. And the investigator to my mind was a correct person. He gave me a cigarette. I told my story. I said what I had to say. I used tactics. While I was in Gradiska, my brother told me, "I'm sure not to survive." "But you must survive because of my children too, and my wife." And he said, "Whatever you have to do, say that I am guilty." So in my statement then I lied to some extent, and I tried to fulfil his wish and to confirm everything so as not to be beaten. And now I can say that that statement was made under pressure and I was beaten before and after I made the statement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm just going to ask you to have a look, please, at your statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, that was copied and handed out to Your Honours in the bundle. It's the one dated July the 2nd, headed "Manjaca POW camp." I think it might be -- I see we have a new member of the registry here. If the bundle is given to me and I'll have a look for it, it's probably quicker. No, it doesn't appear to be there. We've got a -- Your Honours, it may have been handed out --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's not in the bundle.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No. I think it may have been -- when Your Honours were given all the statements, were you given that one as well?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Oh, yes, it may be.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: If not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Let me confirm to you -- yes, indeed it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. I thought --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] ERN 0304 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I'm sorry about that. Are you referring to the document ERN in English 03045352?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That's the one. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm going to ask that that be given to the witness. And I'm going to ask Your Honours to look at the B/C/S copy for obvious reasons as well. If that could be handed to the witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want you to turn it over, please, and have a look at the signatures on the back, first of all, Mr. Filipovic. Apparently it's signed by a gentleman called Dane Lukajic, somebody called Rada Maksimovic, and then your name appears. Is that normally what your signature looks like? I'm sorry, first of all, is that in fact your signature?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is my signature. Only, my signature isn't like this. You can compare all the other signatures you have and which I can make now and you will see that this is a signature done by a hand that couldn't work properly and I only just managed to sign this, but it is my signature.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I just want to ask you about one part of what was put down into that statement. There's a paragraph which states: "Generally speaking, I know nothing about how Kljuc as a whole, the town and its local communes, was armed. Lately, I have also distanced myself from political activity because I realised that what was being done here could only lead to war." Was that true?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This was just to save my life. This is in response to what my brother told me, to play the game and to blame everything on him if necessary. But it's not true. Because I knew a statement like this would save me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. That's all that I want to ask about it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, may that be made Exhibit -- I think we're at -- 1102A and B.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, as I say, Mr. Filipovic, we've had a lot of evidence about Manjaca. But I would like to see if you can -- if you could summarise in a few words, or a sentence or so, what was Manjaca like.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One could talk about Manjaca for months, days, and years. As you insist that I summarise it, all I can say is the difference between Auschwitz, Mathausen, and Manjaca is that over there they had gas chambers and at Manjaca there were no gas chambers. And I said in my statement that the Serbs -- or rather, in my testimony that the Serbs made three mistakes. The second mistake they made was when they put me on a concrete floor. That was the second mistake. If they had put me in a nice bed, I would probably be under the ground. But the cold concrete in a sense healed my injuries. Not just mine, but all the prisoners.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to ask you -- although I've asked you to summarise, I am going to ask you about a couple of things. First of all, you've described how you were beaten by Bulatovic shortly after your arrival. Were you beaten on any further occasions during your stay at Manjaca? And you've told us about the interrogation beatings, yes.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only on one other occasion, because, Your Honours, throughout that time I could not move. I was lying down. And only on one more occasion was I beaten. I think it was on Wednesdays that they would make a roll call and when they call you out -- the stable was about 100 metres long -- you had to run out of the stable. I couldn't do it quickly, so one would get a couple of blows. In Manjaca at first the worst situation was with food. We were hungry over there, thirsty. There was no food. Let me just say that one loaf of bread of 800 grammes would be divided up among 44 men. One can of minced meat or meat pate would be shared by eight men. So you can imagine what it was like. When the first consignment of aid came from Merhamet in Banja Luka, the foot improved a little, but the real improvement came when the International Red Cross took over, and that is when we started getting food. But by then we had become so weak that we were skeletons. I think there is a video cassette showing me. At the time I had recovered a little with the help of one of the prisoners who was the head of the canteen. So when I got to London, I had already gained some 10 kilos, because this lead chef, when his brother was killed, said to himself, "I have to save Muhamed," and so secretly he would bring me sugar and milk so the other prisons wouldn't see it, so that I regained a little weight over there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We're going show the cassette in a moment, Mr. Filipovic. Did you -- in the barn in which you were housed, were other people taken out and beaten?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I remember a detail. There was an active-duty corporal, Sinisa, a Romany from Nis. He was from Serbia proper. He wasn't a Muslim; he was a Serb. He was an active-duty soldier. A junior officer of the so-called JNA. And I saw with my own eyes and counted 94 blows with a police truncheon when Zeljko Bulatovic was beating him. And Zeljko Bulatovic demanding persistently that he should repent, and he said, "I will not repent. I'm not a criminal like you. You will be held accountable sooner or later." And allegedly he was charged that as a corporal he had revealed some major military secrets to Franjo Tudjman. I personally believe there was nothing in it. He bothered them because he was a gypsy and the regime led by the SDS at the time was similar to Naziism and they didn't want gypsies, Muslims, or Croats. They bothered them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, did you receive any medical treatment for your injuries whilst you were at Manjaca, before the International Red Cross arrived?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was taken to the clinic over there. There were three doctors, also detainees only they were physicians. Enis Sabanovic examined me. He took my blood pressure. And my brother took me there, and my brother knew Dr. Sabanovic and Sabanovic measured my blood pressure, and the device showed 0. I had no blood pressure at the time. Omer asked him, "Doctor, do you have any pills to give him?" And the doctor said, "My dear Filipovic, do you know where we are? This is not a hospital." So when you go to the camp, as the clinic was outside the camp where their offices were. So when you enter the camp, tell the cooks that is I said he should be given some red onions and let him drink a lot of water. So I was given a red onion. I ate it like an apple and I drank a lot of water. It is well known that red onions increase blood pressure. And I was given another red onion, so that sometimes when Sabanovic got hold of any pills or painkiller, he would smuggle it in, because he would come back in the evening. He would spend the day over there, and then when he came to the camp either he or Dr. Meho would bring some pills. So the only medical treatment I had was if one of the doctors would give me a painkiller now and then.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Your brother, Mr. Filipovic, I don't know whether you'd prefer not to talk about what happened.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am ready to testify. That is why I came here. I came here to testify.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was your brother in the same barn as yourself?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, until he got in their way, because they realised that my brother was helping the morale of the prisoners. People had become resigned to their fate. They were eating grass. In the daytime people would eat grass they were so hungry. And then my brother would come by and say, "Don't do that. Don't give them pleasure seeing us Muslims eating grass." Some would listen; others would not. But they realised that Omer was improving the morale of the prisoners. After talking to Omer, a prisoner would find it easier to bear the beatings, and so Omer was taken to solitary confinement. In the first spell, for 19 days I think he was beaten there, mistreated. They were so base that in the morning this damn Bulatovic would bring him breakfast and hot tea. Instead of giving it to him - I apologise to the ladies - instead of giving him the tea to drink, he would take off his pants and poor the hot tea over him. He humiliated him in such a way, but Omer would not give in. And on one occasion when we were going for lunch Omer had come out of solitary confinement then upon the insistence of the International Red Cross, because they were told that no one should be kept in solitary confinement non-stop for 19 days. So Omer was let out, and I was going with Omer to have lunch. Bulatovic approached. And I wish to stress that Zeljko Bulatovic called himself Fadil, saying, "You see, I am a balija like you. I am Fadil Bulatovic. But I prefer to serve Mr. Karadzic than Alija Izetbegovic," he would say. However, we knew that he was lying, that this was just to taunt us. And then this Bulatovic went up to Omer and asked him, "So what are you thinking about now, professor?" And Omer answered, in a gentlemanly way, "I am thinking that if I survive Manjaca and am released, I am thinking about the book I shall write." And then he said, "Will there be any place for me in the book?" And he said, "Yes, indeed, Mr. Corporal. You will be the main hero in my book." After that statement, Bula took it out on Omer, not just that very moment. But a few days later he would take out Omer. He would take him for solitary confinement. He would beat him mercilessly and mistreat him in all manner of ways.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The day he died, did you see him?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did see him on the 29th. Omer passed away in the evening of the 28th, and I was allowed on the 29th to see him. So I did see him on the 29th, about 4.00. And when I saw him, I saw him dead. He was absolutely naked. He had been stripped. And on his hand he didn't even have his wedding ring. As my cousin Nihad Filipovic was with me, I said to Nihad, "Examine him closely whether there is a wedding ring." And then according to the Islamic custom, I read a prayer. But Nihad went down again and said, "There's no wedding ring." I bent down and kissed my brother. And if person who was in charge of those two Chetniks - he was an officer, a captain - he came up to me and expressed his condolences and said literally, "Please accept my sincere condolences, and be assured that I am not in favour of these things." And then I said, "Thank you, dear God, that in this fucking Bosnia there is someone who doesn't agree with this. Did they really have to take his wedding ring off?" And then the van took his body and Esad's body without any orders or commands. All the inmates in the camp stood at attention so that the Serbs are afraid of a rebellion. So you -- "this is how you're seeing off your leader, and one day you'll provide a similar sendoff to Alija Izetbegovic." And when Omer was exhumed, when I transferred Omer's body from Banja Luka to Kljuc, I found the wedding ring on Omer's skeleton and I assume that the captain who expressed his condolences forced these other two Chetniks to return the wedding ring, because he knew that they were the people who stripped him and they could -- they were the only ones who could have stolen it. So the wedding ring was found and when he was exhumed, we buried him with the wedding ring. For me the worst moment was when we carried him from Banja Luka to Kljuc and when we opened the coffin. This was the worst moment for me than all the beatings I got at Manjaca.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think we can stop here for the time being. We will have a break of 15 minutes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Filipovic, just one or two further questions on Manjaca. First, the Esad you mentioned, was that Esad Bender?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who died at the same time, or more or less.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 29th.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was he an old friend of the family?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He died on my hands, on my arms in Manjaca. He expired at 5.30 a.m.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what sort of condition was he in when he died in your arms?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was beaten up. He was sick, lifeless. The day before he told me, "I'm bleeding. I am urinating blood." Mujo Sehic, another prison, was a contact person between us because we were not sleeping in this same row. Then Mujo would convey messages to him, his messages to me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there any way that the condition of Omer and Esad could have been unknown to the guards?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, on the night of July 28th, when they beat them up, there were also other prisoners who had been beaten. Then Omer jumped into a minefield and asked Esad Bender to be released, and then he would go out of the minefield. And it would then -- it was very likely for Omer to tread on a mine because he was exhausted. And then the Chetniks would go up. The other prisoners had already been released, and they went to the stable. Then Omer was thrown into a hole. Then he was beaten thoroughly in that hole. And then he was put into solitary confinement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As I say, just two other questions. First, you've spoken about aid coming from Merhamet. Did you know Adil Medic?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever or did he ever speak to you when he came to Manjaca?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When he came to Manjaca, he just waved to me. He was not allowed to contact me. From every stall there was one prisoner who could go and talk to him. From our stable it was Omer. He asked a jacket [as interpreted] and Adil insisted that the representatives of Merhamet and of the other stables should have a talk with Colonel Popovic. And they said that we weren't being beaten in Manjaca. Since my jacket was all bloody, Omer asked to be given my jacket, and this was proof that there was blood in Manjaca and that this was a jacket of one of the inmates, because the jacket was all bloody. And I would encounter Esad a few more times. The arrival of Merhamet was salvation for us. We were fed better, and at the time all the prisoners who could move were waiting at 12.00 or 1.00 in the afternoon, could see the trucks coming. And when they saw food coming, they were in a better mood.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Of the aid that Merhamet delivered, how much more food did that mean that you got?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot express to what extent it was increased, but it was a different form of aid. It in fact -- in this way the Serbs did not have to feed us. They hardly waited for them to come, because they themselves were in a crisis. And even though we received very little food from them, they would use it for themselves and we would eat only the food brought by Merhamet. When we were taken over by the Red Cross, we were better fed in Manjaca than the Chetniks that were securing us. We had three meals. We had a quarter of bread for every meal. And they asked food from us, and they said -- and they said that they were -- that we were being better fed than them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, eventually were you airlifted out of -- or you were taken out of Manjaca and airlifted to England; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I don't remember which day exactly. I think it was the first Saturday. Spaga, who was responsible for the prison, he said, "All the names that I read out should take their personal belongings and should stand here." Amongst them -- I was also amongst them. We waited there. We waited. It became dark. We thought it was a joke. When we had to return to the camp again they told us, "You see, no one really wants you. The Turks should have, in fact, landed on the Banja Luka airport, but they didn't dare." Then Spaga on Tuesday came again. He came to the stable. He said, "All the names I read out should stand." And then my name was read out again. That day it was raining. We went out, and in the meantime the buses came and one of the main investigators said, "You see, without your brethren, the orthodox, nothing will come of you. No one wanted you, not even the Turks." The Russian airplane landed at Banja Luka, and he said, "Your brothers, the orthodox, will take you away." And he told us, "You have to go for treatment." We were guessing where we would be taken. We didn't know where. Some thought we were going to Rovinj, to Croatia. And then we were told the very first time that we would be taken to England. And one of the guards shouted out, "Filipovic, thanks to Mr. Karadzic you are now a free people. You have been -- you have been given abolition. And if someone didn't know what that means, Filipovic explain it to them. And I said that -- in my testimony, I didn't know what to do. I said, "Thanks to Mr. Karadzic, we are also prisoners. If it hadn't been for Karadzic, I would never have seen Manjaca. He told me, "Leave that for later." And then we were put in buses, taken to the Banja Luka airport, and there one bus -- that was one bus and there was another bus coming from Trnopolje, bringing a group of prisoners from there. And 68 of us were then airlifted to London. I would like to explain another detail from Manjaca, because I think it is important. When Bernard Kouchner -- Mr. Bernard Kouchner came, sent from the International Community to examine the conditions in Manjaca, he was -- I was -- I intrigued him. I put my head in a drinking vessel where the cows would drink. And one of the crutches that one of the prisoners gave me put -- I put it under me, and Mr. Kouchner asked Mr. Popovic, "What's the mat we are that prisoner?" Popovic answered straight away, "This one was hit by a horse." I spoke out. I said I wasn't hit by a horse. The lady who translated to Mr. Kouchner translated literally that I was not hit by a horse. Mr. Kouchner was interested. He didn't want to go. And he asked, and I said that I was beaten by an army. And Mr. Popovic asked, "Which army?" I said, "There was only the Serbian army there." "Where"? "In Kljuc, Mali Logor, (redacted)." "Were you beaten in Manjaca too"? But I was incapacitated even before Manjaca. Blank pages inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Pages 9627 to 9631. Then he answered, "Kouchner, now you can see what is important is that he didn't suffer beatings in Manjaca but before Manjaca." I think it is a detail that should be stated.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Once you got to England, did you finally receive proper medical treatment for your injuries?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On September 15th, from the airport we were distributed in different hospitals. There were 68 of us in the Russian plane. It was prepared for us exclusively. There were those who were seriously ill, and the seats had been removed and beds accommodated. On the 15th I was admitted. I was treated -- I was examined on the 16th and at 8.00 in the morning I was operated on. I had three operations on my leg and one on my nose. I apologise. I must add that during my stay in Manjaca the swelling stopped and my brother told me that my nose was broken. So you can imagine how long it took for my swelling to subside, so that my nose could be seen properly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you just tell us, please, as a result of the injuries and the operations, what aftereffects -- we've all seen you limp. What are the aftereffects that you've suffered?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have become a lifetime invalid in my right leg. My right leg is shorter. I have artificial ligaments. I have screws in my knees. Mr. Stallard [phoen], the specialist in England, performed that operation and he told me that if I had come in time, I would have saved you. Now this -- the situation is such that I can just superficially heal you but not heal you totally.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Filipovic, those are the physical injuries that -- the physical aftereffects. If you can, can you tell the Court what those events in 1992 did -- how it affected you as a man.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can say that I'm in fairly good spirits. I'm trying not to -- I'm not a person who seeks revenge. I don't want to seek revenge in the same way that things happened to us. But for me justice is when I see these people in -- prisoners and the investigator who questioned me in Manjaca. He asked me, "Would you seek revenge?" And I said, "No. Personally I would not seek revenge, but I'm waiting for the day when I can see these people on the other side of the bars." And I would like to see the day when my former friend Vinko Kondic is in The Hague.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And finally this: Whilst you were in England, were you invited to take part in a programme made by channel 4 dealing with refugees from Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They asked me if I wished to take part. This is, I might say, the third mistake by the Serbs who allowed me to go for treatment and to become cured, because I said to myself, While you are alive, you will speak the truth and only the truth. And whoever behaved well towards me, I mentioned this. I mentioned Ratko Radojcic and other Serbs who were nice to me. So when I was asked do you want to take part, and in their concept they wanted to make a programme called "Bloody Bosnia." And they wanted to have three stories there, a Muslim, a Serb, and a Croatian story. They wanted to have a refugee from all three sides to tell their version of this story and to have the British audience watch this and judge for themselves what had occurred in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. I'd now like, please, the video that's been handed in to the technicians to be played. Your Honours, before that happens there's a transcript -- it is English, in fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's only the first page. Your Honours got everything, but it's only the first page. And if Mr. Filipovic -- is it on the video? Mr. Filipovic's monitor is on video, is it? Thank you. Sound.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I can't hear any sound.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I've been informed that there is no sound on this tape.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] If there is no sound, how is it that we have a transcript?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: There is sound, Your Honour. I don't know what's happened. I'm afraid to say we asked for an excerpt to be made of it, and I didn't appreciate it -- because I've seen it -- I took it off the original and I didn't appreciate --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So it may have --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm going to ask for the original to be brought down now, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] All right.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Watching it without sound doesn't make sense.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It doesn't, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Apart from the fact that -- even though we have transcript here and it has to be --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No. I think Your Honour ought to hear the proper -- yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] It's confirmation -- would be confirmation of what we have here in any case, even though the --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is it off again? Yes. Sorry. Do we have to wait long for this, Ms. Korner?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, I hope it won't take more than five minute, but it may be just as well if Your Honours rise. We may have to get it from upstairs. I'm sorry about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. So we'll have a short break until the tape arrives. --- Break taken at 4.29 p.m.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm told, Your Honour, that there is sound.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] This is definitely mine. That's probably because I have this here. Okay. Let's proceed. There's something that has -- something that has gone wrong here.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we stop. Can we have the sound. Your Honour, I'd like the video stopped until -- Can we go back, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we go back to the beginning, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Stop.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we go back to the beginning of the video.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please take us back to the beginning of the video, a short rewind. [Videotape played]. At the time we were inseparable. In those days it never mattered that my brother Omer and I were Muslims and our best friend Vinko was the Serb. Our families lived next door to each other. Every weekend we'd eat together. Our children would play together. Then the war came to Bosnia. Omer had become a prominent man in our town Kljuc. Then, when the Serbs captured Kljuc, our friend Vinko became chief of police. Vinko of course knew all about Omer's position and he must have seen him as a threat. One night the Serb militia came for us. Omer, me, and all the other Muslim men were arrested. But it was Omer they really wanted. We were taken to Manjaca camp. There the guards would come for Omer at dusk, beat him for hours, then return him in the motor vehicles. Each day he grew weaker. One day Vinko entered the camp in his police uniform. He looked at me. Vinko knew what was happening there. He knew what was happening to the man he'd once called his best friend. The last day they came for Omer everyone knew he was going to die. Omer waved to me and said goodbye. When I close my eyes at night, I see him waving again and again. When they carried me off the plane in London, I didn't feel relieved, just helpless. I wondered if I'd ever see my family again. Of course I knew I wouldn't see Omer. He was buried the same day I left Bosnia. I often think back to the old days when Omer, Vinko, and I would eat together. I ask myself, what was really going through Vinko's mind as we sat around the table laughing together. My Red Cross certificate says I'm 38. It is not true. I'm really only one year old, because it's only in the last year I've learned what people are really like.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's all I'd ask of Mr. Filipovic. I'd ask that the video be made Exhibit 1103 and the transcript 1103.1 and .2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I understand there is no objection on the part of the Defence. Okay. So it's so admitted. And that's all. That brings your examination-in-chief to the end.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, that's all I ask.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I just wanted to make sure. Who's going to go first?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I, Your Honours, say something?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There's a mistake here. Those are people from channel 4. I was telling them the story, and I don't know how it came about that he said "one night Vinko came to the camp." Vinko did not come to the camp, so I don't know how he came to say that. So I just wanted to make that correction. Everything else is all right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I thank you. Now, as I tried to explain to you the first -- the very first time you sat on that chair in this courtroom, after the examination-in-chief by the Prosecution, the Defence, both accused, are entitled according to our rules to cross-examine you. In cross-examination -- the first cross-examination will be that on behalf of Radoslav Brdjanin. And the attorney who will be cross-examining you is the lead attorney, Mr. John Ackerman. Now, I think I have already explained to you also that these gentlemen who are defending the accused are doing their duty here. They are being paid by this Tribunal to do their duty, and that is to defend their clients. Because like everyone else, the accused here are presumed to be innocent until they are proved guilty. So I leave you now in the hands of Mr. Ackerman. And my advice to you, again, is to answer the question, the whole question, and nothing but the question. Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Cross-examined by Mr. Ackerman:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Filipovic.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to start by telling you that I and I think everyone in this courtroom feels a great deal of sorrow and sympathy with you for what happened to you and your brother and your family and everything else that you've just explained to us. And I hope that you'll accept that in the spirit that I offer it to you. I want to begin by talking to you about the elections that occurred in --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I seem to be having trouble with my earphones or something, Your Honour. I can't hear half the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Just a minute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can you hear me? No. Could it be the sound? Because there has been some --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: No. It's something wrong with the earphones. They just come on and come on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Usher, could --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Let me get another pair.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: There are plenty around, so that's not a problem. Let's try. Can you hear me? Okay. Let's see. Can your assistant hear me?

utterances.speaker: MS. JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If there is a problem, Mr. Ackerman, perhaps -- exactly. You're going to switch places. Alternatively I was going to suggest to you to move to the -- to the other -- yes. Let's see if it works now. Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good. So there is nothing wrong with your hearing, as I started suspecting for a while. So let's go ahead.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, following the -- I want to go back to that time when the multi-party elections were held and just kind of some background. Following those elections, the SDS wound up winning over 50 per cent of the seats in the Municipal Assembly of Kljuc, did they not?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that meant that the SDS controlled the assembly in any matter requiring a simple majority vote; correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that result of those elections, those democratic elections, was not acceptable to you and your brother, was it?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, isn't it the case that -- I just have to find it. Just give me a second -- you gave a statement to the Prosecutor on 28 August, 2002, here in The Hague. You spoke with Ms. Korner and Mr. Ackheim. And I'd ask the Prosecutor to give you a copy of that statement so you can see what I'm referring to. If you look on the second page. On the English version, it's the third paragraph, beginning with "This would be done by the Serbs being a majority." Do you see the part I'm referring to?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told the Prosecutor -- you were talking about the results of the elections and the Serbs have been a majority in the assembly and that you believed that would be detrimental to the Muslims. You said "This would be done by the Serbs being a majority through passing laws and issue decisions depriving the non-Serbs of their land and property." And then I'll skip a sentence. "During a press conference, my brother and myself carried a yellow ribbon on our sleeves. We told the audience that we would end up like the Jews of Kljuc if the Serbs had their way." That's true, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: True.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you mean when you said you would end up like the Jews of Kljuc?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have to elaborate now and say at length what it is I expected. I'm sufficiently intelligent and educated to know what happened to the Jews during the Second World War. We knew what would happen to us. We would be disenfranchised, individuals killed, individuals deprived of their property. They would be segregated. We need not necessarily have had to have yellow ribbons like the Jews in the Second World War. Maybe a green ribbon or some other ribbon would be given to us, but we had to be marked, because a state was being established in which the Serbs were to have exclusive power, and that is what I meant at the time. As for what I said about property, I can say on well-founded grounds that we lived in a state in which the Serbs were dominant and we were always deprived of property by the reforms of King Aleksandar then the Rankovic reforms who had influence over Tito. We were deprived of our property. We Filipovics had plenty of land we could boast of. However, after the end of the reforms, we had seven or eight dulums left. And we had thousands of dulums of land. King Aleksandar took our land, and the same applies to the Assembly of the ARK of Krajina. So that is what I meant to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] We'd like to know what a dulum is. A dulum, I understand, is a measure. It's like --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it is. It is 1.000 square metres of land.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What you said in your statement, this fear that you had of winding up like the Jews of Kljuc, resulted from the Serbs being a majority through passing laws and issuing decisions. And I take it that it was your position they could do that because they had won the election and controlled the assembly.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As an attorney, you know that some decisions are made by relative majority and some by an absolute majority. And according to the statute, for some decisions they need add two-thirds majority and they didn't have it. And that is why we were in parliament, because we could prevent some decisions from being taken, because the SDS did not have a two-thirds majority. And for all other decisions for this a simple majority was needed, the other parties didn't need to be present. The SDS would make its decisions having 31 deputies in parliament.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did you and your brother hold this press conference where you wore yellow ribbons on your sleeves and talked about the minority status of the Muslim people? Where did you have that press conference?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the office of the cultural centre where the Muslim Bosniak organisation had its premises.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I take it it was attended by representatives of the media?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A press conference was called for the press. So all correspondents of newspapers working in Kljuc, then a reporter from Radio Kljuc, and from our local newspapers, who worked together with Radio Kljuc. All the other correspondents working for other BH newspapers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what you and your brother said at that conference was at least to some extent reported in the media in Kljuc, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You didn't see the newspaper? You didn't listen to the radio? You didn't know if they paid attention to you or not?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did listen. Only, I don't know whether they did, whether it was published just then. I don't know whether they published it. I think that something was published. I'm convinced that it was published, but I didn't hear it with my own ears.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the purpose of this, of course, was to -- was to try to stir up the Muslim people of Kljuc and get them frightened of the Serbs and to get them to support you and your brother in the campaign you were waging?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not true. The Muslim people were already scared, and they didn't need to be frightened further. They were so frightened that they didn't know what to do. And this was just to open the eyes of those who still saw the Serbs as their neighbours, their kums, and their friends.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the yellow ribbon on your sleeves was designed to emphasize that, I take it?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not true. We didn't need to emphasise anything. I don't know why anyone should be bothered by that. We just wanted to say that we would feel in a state being minded by the SDS, just as the Jews felt in Nazi Germany. The course of events has proven that we were right. We were persecuted. Our sisters, mothers were raped. Our children were expelled from school. We were forced to go to school, to teach our children to make the cross and to bow to St. Sava. Simply something was imposed upon us that we didn't want. It's the same as if -- Mr. Ackerman, I don't know of what faith you are. I am a Muslim. I cannot impose upon you something that you don't want. You have your democratic right to be what you wish to be, and that is my right too, and the SDS wanted to deprive us of that right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you -- among other things, you believed as a people, as an ethnic Muslim population that you had a right of self-determination to determine your own destinies and not be governed by a majority with which you did not agree.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was guaranteed by the constitution. You know that the constitution is the highest law of a nation, and the constitution guaranteed this to us, because we are a nation. According to the last constitution, we had that right. We were until then Muslims. We had the same right as the Serbs and the Croats because the constitution says that the Muslims, Serbs, and Croats are the nations of Bosnia-Herzegovina; therefore, Bosnia-Herzegovina was not Serbian, Croatian, or Muslim, but Bosnia and Herzegovina was the state of the citizens of Bosnia-Herzegovina, that is, of Serbs, Croats, and Muslims. And the Serbs prohibited this. They deleted everything that was Bosnian and gave the prefix "Serbian." If it was a fir wood, they would call it a Serbian fir wood. That's just a joke. For them everything was Serbian.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think I would like you to answer my question, and that was this: Did you believe as a member of a -- an ethnic minority that you had the right to govern --

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were not a national minority.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
