utterances.text: I'm not talking about national. I'm talking -- I'm talking about Kljuc now. In Kljuc you were a minority. Did you believe in Kljuc that you had the right to govern yourselves and determine your own destinies? That's my question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And may I add, because you didn't finish your question, Mr. Ackerman, your question also said "and not be governed by a majority with which you did not agree."

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wish in connection with this answer to say that we are not a minority. We are an equal nation to the Serbian nation. Therefore, Mr. Ackerman says "you were a member of a minority." We know what a national minority is. We are not a minority. We are a nation, an equal nation. According to the census of 1991, we were almost equal in number to the Serbs. I was saying earlier on in my testimony that if it hadn't been for certain policies in 1962, we would have been the majority nation in Kljuc.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You still have not answered my question. When the Serbs won the election, the SDS won the election in Kljuc, and acquired the majority of the seats in the assembly, did you, having less than a majority of the seats - you, meaning the members of the MBO and the SDA - feel like you had a right of self-determination, I'll call it, that is, to govern yourselves and not be governed by a majority with which you did not agree? Is that what you believed?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was guaranteed to us by the constitution, Mr. Ackerman. I don't know how to answer you. That was guaranteed us by the constitution, and we just requested that the constitution be observed. I don't want you to take me to some other question, because this is something -- the SDS needed a two-thirds majority. They implemented certain things. We were not afraid of anything. We didn't fear the SDS rule, but we wanted them to rule in a democratic manner. At an interparty meeting we make certain agreements and that's fine. But we were bothered by the way in which they implemented their decisions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... And I wouldn't press it any further.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm going to something else, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I believe he's not answered my question, but he's not going to and I'm going to give up.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You and your brother organised the Kljuc version of the Patriotic League, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Together with some other friends of ours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And your efforts to organise and arm the Muslim people of the Kljuc municipality met with considerable success, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Why, it depends how you look at it. You have been able to see from my testimony how successful we were. But we tried. We didn't have a big ally like the Serbs, called the JNA, to arm us. If we had NATO or someone else, maybe we would have done better.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, you actually acquired arms. You armed a number of people who were your followers, your adherents. And the Patriotic League -- well, let me stop there, because that was a question I just asked you. You gained a lot of adherents and you armed a lot of people, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My answer to this question of yours, Mr. Ackerman, would be that it was the Serbs who were more successful in doing that by their moves, because from one day to the next they would take a move which the -- which pushed the people closer to us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, did you hear me ask you a question about how successful the Serbs were arming themselves? I didn't ask you that, did I?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't answer either. I said that the Serbs assisted our people more in their efforts. They brought it home to the people more, they did, than we did from the leadership of the SDA and the MBO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You should take my advice, Mr. Filipovic. I advised you already, answer the question, the whole question, and nothing but the question. Don't go beyond the parameters of the question, because you will end up in a labyrinth. The question was a very simple one: Do you consider that you were successful in organising and arming your people? The answer should have been yes or no.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, we were not sufficiently successful. I don't know why it matters if I add that we didn't have allies, but we were not successful enough.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That explains why you weren't successful, but I would stop there. Why draw comparisons with the Serbs and give further explanations. Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The Patriotic League, Mr. Filipovic, was a -- a Bosnia-wide organisation. It wasn't just Kljuc. It was a large organisation. Every municipality in Bosnia, or nearly every one, 65, 70 thousand armed people at least. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It existed in every municipality, but I don't know how many members it had.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you and your brother attend meetings of the Patriotic League outside the Kljuc municipality?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did either of you go to the meeting at -- I think it's Mehurici by Travnik for a military forum that Sefer Halilovic organised for the Patriotic League? Did either of you attend that?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know that the Patriotic League had nine regional headquarters?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know what the regional headquarters was for the Kljuc municipality?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There came a day -- and I'm moving along now -- did there not when in the Municipal Assembly of Kljuc, after the multi-party elections, that an item was suggested on the agenda regarding a proposal to join the Autonomous Region of Krajina? Correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And at that point the assembly members from the SDA and the MBO were still participating in the assembly, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it was the joint position of the SDA and the MBO that the Kljuc municipality should not join the Autonomous Region of Krajina; correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when it came -- became clear that there was going to be a vote and it was going to pass, all of the representatives from the SDA and the MBO left the assembly, and then you proclaimed the municipality of Bosanski Kljuc; correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Wasn't this an illegal rebellion against the legally established democratic government of Kljuc?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wasn't illegal because we believed that the law passed by the state of Bosnia-Herzegovina was law, and the SDS implemented decisions which were not supported by the official authorities in Sarajevo, and we supported the decisions of the official authorities in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The decision was made by the representatives elected by the people of Kljuc, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which decision?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The decision to join the Autonomous Region of Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But an Autonomous Region of Krajina in Bosnia-Herzegovina needed to be voted by the parliament of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The people -- the decision was made by the elected representatives of the people of the Kljuc municipality, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Without our support. The decision was taken by representatives of one people only, by the decision of the Serbs. The decision was taken to join the Autonomous Region.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I don't know if you follow other democratic legislatures around the world, but in my country lots of decisions are made by republicans only but we all have to live with them. That's the democratic system.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: What's the question?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what you're saying is that if you don't like the decision made by the majority, then you can go off and form your own --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman, I correct you here. He did explain two things. First he explained that the decision to -- for Kljuc to join the Autonomous Region of Krajina and also for the creation of the Autonomous Region of Krajina should have been forthcoming from the parliament of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, don't -- Your Honour, please don't treat that, Your Honour, as if that's a truthful answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, I'm not treating that as a truthful answer, but that's what he told you. So in actual fact he drew a line where the legality according to him stood. In other words, he explained to you in abundantly clear terms that according to him they were in the right, they acted legally, while the SDS in the Municipal Assembly of Kljuc acted illegally. So --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, I understand, Your Honour. And I'm about to accept that reasoning on his part.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm not saying it's good or bad.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm not saying -- but he did explain to you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, just let me ask you this. The Judge has taken us a couple of steps down if road. But now that we're there, we'll take it the whole way. What you did with your abandonment of the Assembly in Kljuc and the proclamation of the municipality of Bosanski Kljuc is virtually identical, isn't it, to that moment when the SDS members left the republican assembly because they were opposed to a resolution calling for independence of Bosnia-Herzegovina and created the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina? They did the same thing with the same legal basis that you had for what you did. Right?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But the difference is that we weren't threatening anyone, as opposed to when Mr. Karadzic abandoned the parliament and said that one nation would disappear from the face of the earth. And he was referring to the Muslims. And when we walked out of the Municipal Assembly of Kljuc, we didn't threaten anyone. We just wanted to support the laws of the State of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, actually the reason that you did that was because the Muslims in Kljuc and all across Bosnia-Herzegovina were not prepared to settle for a minority status. They wanted to be in control and they wanted to carry the day. They wanted to be able to cast the deciding votes on everything. Now, that's what was going on, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not right. We wanted to remain in Yugoslavia. We in Yugoslavia were not a majority nation but we were recognised as a nation. And we wanted to live in a state in which we had been living for centuries. We felt that we couldn't live in Yugoslavia if Slovenia and a part of Croatia leaves that country.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman, we need to have a break now.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yeah. It's a good time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: 15 minutes, resuming at five past -- 5.35. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: May I proceed, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Filipovic, when we were talking a few moments ago about the acts of legislative bodies, you talked about the constitution that protected a nation like the Muslims, the Serbs, the Croats. And in fact what that constitution provided, did it not, was that no -- no majority could make a decision against the legitimate interests of one of those constitutive bodies, constitutive peoples?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's true, isn't it? And that's what you were talking about when you talked about the constitution?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I answered that question. And I said that as far as I knew, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when we talk about what happened in the republican assembly regarding the issue of independence, the Croats and the Muslims announced that they were going to make a decision against what the Serbs said was their -- an important interest of the Serbs, which was in violation of the constitution, the same way that you and I talked about what happened in Kljuc. And that's why the Serbs walked out, because the constitution was being violated by the Muslims and the Croats in insisting on voting for that against the interests of the Serb people. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wasn't the Serbs that walked out of the assembly. It was the representatives of the SDS. But other Serbs from other political parties remained who were carrying out their function of deputy in parliament. So my answer is that only the representatives of the SDS walked out, and perhaps representatives of some other parties too - perhaps Seselj's party.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, when we broke a few minutes ago, the question I asked you was -- you took the position you took in the municipality of Bosanski Kljuc because all across Bosnia-Herzegovina at that time, Muslims were not willing to find themselves in a minority situation. They wanted to be the majority and be in control. And I think you told me that that wasn't the case. So I'd like you to look, please, at Exhibit 854, P854. Now, this document, sir, you've looked at earlier in your testimony. This was the -- it's a Radio Kljuc report of a meeting that was held in Kljuc. The speaker was Professor Muhamed Filipovic, and he was talking about who is destroying Bosnia. And if you look at the third paragraph, he said, according to the radio record: "Slovenia and Croatia's decision to secede from Yugoslavia would only make the situation more complicated for all and particularly for Bosnia and Herzegovina, which cannot consent to agreements like the one between Cvetkovic and Macek and the way they are making arrangements with --" and the sentence is not finished, "where Muslims would be a minority in a rump Yugoslavia and we do not want to live in this kind of Yugoslavia." Now, that's what Professor Muhamed Filipovic said at this meeting; correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is an interpretation by a journalist, but I agree on this report of his to Radio Kljuc. We did not wish to live in a Yugoslavia without Croatia and Slovenia. According to the constitution of 1974, this was not Yugoslavia for us, and this also applies to the other constitutions. I can say today that I wish that the Yugoslavia of then existed, the Yugoslavia based on the constitution of 1974.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Further on down, if you go down to a paragraph that begins with the word "talking," Professor Filipovic said that "It cannot be tolerated. That there are some people in Bosnia-Herzegovina who recognise it and others who do not, as Serbia is sovereign in its own constitution, so Bosnia-Herzegovina, otherwise it will not be equal and Muslims will be outvoted. BH authority must function over every inch of the country of BH." Correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot see that in my text.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It should be the last paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I just read it through?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please. Take your time.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Here it is clearly stated. It is stated, and I said -- and it is only logical that on the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina that the BH authority must be in control and that there should be six equal republics, equal -- with equal rights or states, however you like to put it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There was a plan, was there not, to achieve majority status on the part of the Muslims by force of arms if necessary, wasn't there?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you look, please, at Exhibit - I'll make sure I've got the right would you please - Exhibit DB95.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Could we ask what DB95 is. Because we don't have it -- you don't have it either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] No, we don't either. And I don't think it can be right. DB95?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes. You should have it, because it was given to everybody much earlier today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] It hasn't been --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It just wasn't distributed. We turned it in and ...

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It wasn't given to us, Mr. Ackerman, so we should --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm sorry, it should have been distributed long ago. We just didn't get it done.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: We have -- we have three more new exhibits, Your Honour, and I'd ask that the registry distribute those to you and the Prosecutor at this point so we don't do this again.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, the document you're looking at is a document that really has two dates on it. I think the operative date is 29 April, 1992. It's a document that appears to have been issued by the Minister of Internal Affairs of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Mr. Alija Delimustafic. Do you know that Alija Delimustafic was in fact the minister of the internal affairs in Bosnia-Herzegovina in April of 1992?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think the problem, sir, is you're not close enough to the microphones and they're having a hard time hearing your answers. This document is addressed to the chief of all security services centres to the chief of all public security stations, and to the secretary of the Secretariat of the Interior in Sarajevo. It instructs those organisations to take all necessary steps and action within their jurisdiction to assure implementation of the order of the Territorial Defence staff commander of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. This order -- and then the next paragraph: "This order regarding implementation of the decision of the Presidency of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina." It deals with the imminent withdrawal of JNA troops from Bosnia-Herzegovina and requests that, in paragraph 1, "All roads in the territory of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina being used by units of the former JNA for pulling out materiel and equipment are to be completely blocked in direct coordination with the Ministry of the Interior. Larger areas with military installations from which they are trying to pull out materiel and equipment are to be blocked by using various man-made and natural obstacles, which shall be guarded by the units of the Territorial Defence of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Unannounced convoys of former JNA units and convoys without MUP escort shall not be allowed to leave the barracks or to communicate within the territory of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina." Now, those were all measures, weren't they, sir, to -- for the TO of Bosnia-Herzegovina to take control of the weaponry that was in the hands of the JNA troops that were leaving the country; correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The JNA was not retreating from Bosnia-Herzegovina. It was withdrawing from Croatia, and it was going into Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, aren't you aware that there was a time when Milosevic ordered the withdrawal of the JNA from Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was Mr. Milosevic's game. I know that the JNA was coming from Croatia to Bosnia and Herzegovina. If Kljuc is understood as part of Bosnia and Herzegovina. I was in Kljuc. I told you what I could watch, only the first paragraph of Television Sarajevo. There were no military facilities, military facilities in Kljuc, except that the barracks that was being built in Laniste. I don't know if there were other barracks or other facilities in other parts. All I know is that they were coming.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, you've told us that your only interest in arming yourselves in Kljuc and presumably throughout Bosnia-Herzegovina was to defend yourselves. Would you look, please, at paragraph 4. "The planning and launching of combat activities throughout the territory of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina is to be accelerated and these activities are to be coordinated with the Territorial Defence staffs of the region, district, and Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. In the course of planning combat activities, extensive measures should be planned for protecting the people and the property of the citizens of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina." That's what that document says, does it not?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it does. But it is the first time that I see this document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did anybody ever tell you about having received it?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Would you tell me what is the date of this document?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, you've got it there in front of you. It says "29 April, 1992."

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At a meeting. But when was it sent? What does this 11th of May mean?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I can't -- I can't answer that question. I don't know that. It says that that date was added by hand in the upper right-hand corner. It may have to do with when it was sent somewhere. I don't know. I don't think any of us do. My question is: Did anybody ever --

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: So the meeting of the Presidency was on the 29th, but I don't know when the document was then sent out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My question was: Did anybody ever tell you that they had received this document?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was this document the basis, if you know, for any of the blockading activities that were being done by the Muslim people in the Kljuc municipality?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Mr. Ackerman, we didn't have a document addressed to the public security station. Public security was under the control of the SDS, so there was no way of sending that document. I see the document for the very first time, and someone would have mentioned it then.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to completely change -- I'm finished with that document now. Thank you. I'm going to a completely new subject now. On the first day of your testimony you were questioned by Ms. Korner about before the multi-party elections and the difficulties that came from that, about what the relationships were like between the various groups in the Kljuc municipality, how Muslims and Croats and Serbs got along with each other. And your answer to her was - and I'm going to quote it for you - "it's all so mixed that it's impossible to really separate individual ethnic groups"; right?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And her question was about 1990. 1990 was, if my math is correct, 45 years after the end of World War II, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if your calculations are right, then it is that year. 1945, 1990.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And during World War II, you've described for us and many other witnesses have the situation that obtained in the Krajina area during the war with the -- the horrible slaughter of many Serbian people by Ante Pavelic's group. You talked about them. And that all happened in that period 45 years before 1990, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That happened during World War II.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you know that thousands of Serbs were slaughtered in the -- in the Krajina area during World War II, don't you?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only thousands of Serbs. All the victims were Communist. They were Muslims, Croats, Serbs, gypsies. The Ustashas killed those who did not think like them. They killed an Ustasha Croat if he did not support their government.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, the -- yeah, you're right. It was the Ustasha that were doing it, but there was also a quite well-known Muslim SS unit too, wasn't there?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wasn't even conceived then. I was born in 1955.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you heard that there was a Muslim SS unit?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm really not -- I'm not trying to establish any history in the sense that it explains anything. What I'm trying to say is this: How long was it, if you know, after 1945 before these groups were able to develop the close relationships that you talk about in 1990? How many years did that take before that got itself patched up?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could say that in Yugoslavia there was a regime, a Communist regime that held things under control. The police force was powerful. So was the army. This was under the command of Marsal Josip Broz Tito, and he quickly succeeded in achieving that, because his thesis was "brotherhood and unity." So I don't know when it was, because I was a child. For as long as I can remember we lived what nowadays is known as co-existence. We co-existed with our neighbour, Serbs and Croats. According to the tales of my parents, it was the same. My father would frequently say to us children, "I was a rich man in the kingdom, but I never ate so well as I did during Tito's rule."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it's your sense that that happened rather quickly after the war, partly because of the -- the force of Tito?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think it was relatively quickly. It needed time, because it took time for the Marsal to capture Draza Mihajlovic with his troops and police and the others -- other renegades. So we would need to remind ourselves of the history when Kalabic, Braza Mihajlovic, and the other Ustasha extremists were arrested, when Tito captured them. It was after that that life became normal.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. And when you finally get to 1990, what you told us the -- and you're not alone. Many other witnesses have told us this. There was -- your words, "It's so mixed that it's really impossible to separate individual ethnic groups," that there was a lot of intermarriage, that you all celebrated each other's holidays, things of that nature. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. In my own family I have a sister-in-law that is a Serb.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd like you to look at the map that is P1097.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Can I see it before you take it over there? Yes, that's it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, if we can back up so we can see most of the map, that might be helpful. That's fine. Now, sir, if you look at the -- the ethnic map of the Kljuc municipality. And this isn't designed to be mathematically precise, but what you see there is a section of the Kljuc municipality where the villages and hamlets are all green, don't you?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see some marked in green and some in blue and some in black.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. And the ones that are green you have told us and the map indicates are -- are Muslim villages. And I think you've told us that in some of those villages there might have been one Serb family or something like that. But they are virtually 100 per cent Muslim villages, aren't they?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And if you look at -- down south of Kljuc, all of the blue villages, those are all characterised as Serb villages, aren't they?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, according to the 1991 census.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I think you'd agree that there are very few Muslims living in any of those villages that are in blue, or that there were in 1990.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In 1990, Mr. Ackerman. But you're prompting me to say that Zablace, Rastoka, Orahovljani at the end of the Second World War, these were villages with majority Muslim populations, Sitnica, Orahovljani. They have now gone to Mrkonjic Grad, Kopjenica. They're no longer in Kljuc municipality. Srebrenica is missing here near Ribnik. So through many years and thanks to the moves we've been talk about for so long, people moved out and these became majority Serb settlements.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you just look at the map and the colours on that map, that doesn't really match one your assertion that "It's all so mixed that it's impossible to separate individual ethnic groups," does it?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't agree with you because -- where's Kopjenica, for example? Find the village of Kopjenica. It is a 100 per cent Serb village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why -- can you explain to us if these -- if there is such ethnic harmony why the Muslims all seem to live in their own villages and the Serbs all seem to live in their own villages, they don't live together.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I keep trying to explain to you, but you either don't want to understand, because a Muslim was chased out of Rastoka, Gornji Ribnik, Zablace, Orahovljani, he had nowhere else to go but he went to Kljuc. He couldn't go from Sitnica. Where? To Ratkovo? So he had to go to Kljuc, and that's where he went, just as now that I have been expelled and all the Muslims from Kljuc. Where should we go? If we had gone to Banja Luka, we would have been killed in Banja Luka. We were expelled to Travnik, and the people expelled from Kljuc arrived in Travnik and were put up there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yeah. But this -- this map is the ethnic make-up of the Kljuc municipality before there was any war or anything like that, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think we've -- we've mentioned this before. This was Mr. Inayat's best estimate of -- but we haven't actually got the complete figures, so provided Mr. Ackerman is just saying there's a majority, but we can't say that there weren't Serbs living in what is shown as Muslim villages without actually getting the actual figures.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, he's actually -- you're correct. And he's actually testified that a couple of those villages that are green -- those Muslim villages actually had a Serb family in them.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But it was put as the question. I'm sorry, but the only reason I interrupted -- excuse me for just one moment. The only reason I interrupted is this map is the ethnic make-up. Yes, but not in the way --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I think in a way, Mr. Ackerman, Ms. Korner is correct. And if I remember well, the witness also in the beginning of his testimony did explain that there was a difference between villages and big cities where -- in big cities sort of there was a -- everyone from all ethnic groups living together, but not so in the -- in the small villages and small towns. That's if I remember correctly. You know, I mean, it's -- I don't know how much important this is to you, but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I started -- I started my questioning about this with the proposition that with regard to this map that I knew it was not mathematically precise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And so I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Anyway, I mean, you're free to continue if you want to.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think I've made my point; I hope.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to -- in your testimony on the first day - it's page 9300 of the transcript - let me just remind you with it. You talked about after the elections and the SDS winning the majority of the seats. You said as a result of that, they took over all of the institutions of power which have decisive power, being the military, the police, and money. My question is simple: When you say they took over the institution having to do with money, what is that institution? What do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The tax administration, the SDK.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... I'd like you to look now at Exhibit P3. Now, this document, sir, is dated April 10th of 1991, is it not?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can we have it put on the ELMO, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go ahead. Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The date that's contained in the -- the Serbo-Croat version of this document is 10 April, 1991, but it clearly is not that date. Can you by looking at it and looking at the context of it give us your best estimate of the date of the document.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What do you know about this document?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said earlier on what I thought of this document. This document shows that a decision was confirming a previous decision to join the Community of Municipalities of Banja Luka, and I claim that it is not legally valid because if it was legally valid, it needed to be entered into all the registers of the municipality. And I said what I thought earlier on. So this was just a decision whereby the president of the municipal assembly, Jovo Banjac, formally informed the gentlemen in Banja Luka that Kljuc continued to be in ARK Krajina and this was not something that was discussed in the parliament of Kljuc at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And so would it be fair to say that this document was probably issued very close to the time that the vote was taken in the Kljuc Assembly to join the Autonomous Region of Krajina and when you all walked out of the assembly? Does it appear to be a document from about that time?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I wouldn't be able to say. I think it dates to -- back to an earlier period because this went on for a long time, these debates.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, it does mention the Autonomous Region of Krajina, doesn't it? It actually calls it the Autonomous Region of Bosanska Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's what I've said. I've answered that question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it certainly didn't predate the formation of ARK. It has to be after that. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Autonomous Region of Bosanska Krajina was formed, and they considered Kljuc to be a part of that region. However, officially when it was actually established, the exact date, I don't know, and I consider this decision to come from the period when the Autonomous Region was formed and after that, because they needed to check whether Kljuc was in the Autonomous Region. And then Mr. Banjac sent this decision, saying that the previous decision was being confirmed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. I'm finished with that document. I'd like you to look now at P855. This is another document you saw on the first day of your testimony, and it's -- I think it's a Radio Kljuc document, but it -- it advertises a memorial service to be held on August 2nd at the Orthodox church in Kljuc in memory of the victims of the events of July and August 1941. And you'll recall having seen it earlier in your testimony. And the question that was asked of you about that was the effect that this had on the -- the Muslim people of Kljuc and the suggestion that this was designed to -- to frighten and scare the Muslim people so that they would leave town and not feel comfortable in the area. And did you agree with that proposition, that that's what that was for?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree. This document proves that the SPS and the SDS were working together.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you agree with what I suggested was the -- one of the purposes of it; correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So in your view at least, there was a motive among the leadership of the SDS and the Serb people in Kljuc to -- to frighten and intimidate in some ways the Muslim people to try to cause them to leave the area.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When -- are you asking me to answer that?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, I'm asking you to answer that. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that I agreed that this was one of the theses intended to frighten us in Kljuc, because when the war started revenge was taken of us because of the lost battle at Kosovo in 1398, with which we had absolutely no common, because we are Bosnians. And at Kosovo Polje, the war was between the Turks and medieval Serbia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me ask you this: You just talked about that period after 1945, that Yugoslavia was a Communist country; correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a Communist country, right up to 1990.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. And a Communist country in one form or another - some more stringent than others - either discouraged, prohibited, prevented, or punished religion, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not true. It was not prohibited. The Communists simply had their own theory. If you want to be a member of the League of Communists, you can't be a manager if you were not a member. Religion was not prohibited. It was allowed in the Communist state. Who wanted to could go to pray, but there were three nations living in Bosnia-Herzegovina in Kljuc; two nations expressed their religious feelings, whereas one nation, that is, the Serbian nation, leaned more towards the Communist Party. They were greater Communists than we were while they needed it. And I'm sure that the days will come when the Serbs will be greater Bosnians than we are.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it is your position that religion was freely practiced without penalty in Yugoslavia throughout the Communist era?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But you couldn't hold a managerial post and be a believer, but an ordinary worker and an ordinary man in the street was free to go to the church or to a mosque.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, but that changed in 1990. Then you could hold a managerial post and participate in religious activities, couldn't you?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And perhaps for the first time in 45 years it was possible to have a fitting memorial that everyone could attend for those who were killed during that war, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Only let me say again, among those victims there were not just Serbs. There were quite a number of Muslims that were killed by the Ustasha.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There's something I'm very curious about, and maybe you can help us understand it. If it was as you say a position of the SDS and the Serbs to do things to frighten the Muslim people into leaving, can you explain why it is on that tape that we saw yesterday that the interviews of the Muslim people, which you said were coerced, that they were forced to say these things, had the exact opposite design. And that is you don't have to worry about the Serbs in Kljuc. They are wonderful people. They've treated us perfectly. There's no problems. You can feel safe here. It seems to me that had exactly the opposite motive, to make the Muslims feel like it was okay to stay. Can you explain to me -- I mean, how do you reconcile those two things? Can you?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you should ask Mr. Zubcevic Omer. He is currently in America, and he's ashamed of that very statement. And to this date he hasn't come to Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, but he's not the one that's responsible, according to you, for the content of that statement. You said that the Serb authorities forced him to say those things and forced the other Muslim that was interviewed to say those things, comforting things, things to make the Muslims of Kljuc feel safe. How does that square with your contention that what they were trying to do was frighten the Muslims? How do you reconcile those two? I'm not going to ask him. I'm asking you. You're the witness.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that Mr. Emir Kapetanovic made this statement, and maybe the next day or the day after he appeared at Manjaca. If he was doing well, why didn't he stay and play basketball in Kljuc? So if everything was fine and he was playing basketball, why didn't he go on playing basketball? Why did he crop up at Manjaca?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, it's time to conclude for the day, sir, and we'll continue this tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, just before we conclude, on the exhibits. I've just -- oh, yes, first of all - and it all relates to the same exhibit - I'd made the transcripts of the last video we saw .1 and -- I'm sorry, whatever I'd made them. But anyhow, could they be made .1A and .1B to keep them consistent with the rest. Now, just -- this has been happening over and over again, but today it's so obvious that I think we're going to try and put a stop to it. Mr. Ackerman and sometimes Madam Fauveau are reproducing exhibits that we've already given numbers to as Defence exhibits. And it's going to be -- Mr. Ackerman is always concerned about not confusing the transcript. Because the very exhibit I've produced, Mr. Ackerman now wants to produce as DB99 -- 98. So can I suggest that we stick to the number it was given today rather than giving it an added extra number of DB98.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, yes. But see, I did that before you did. I made it DB98 before you made it whatever you made it. So you're the one -- you're the one that's grabbing my exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, but Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: But it's not complete. I'm only interested in the first page.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, that's right. And it's only the first page that should be exhibited. I know that everybody was given a copy of that huge bundle, but that's the only --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Well, I suggest you sort this amongst yourselves, Because I mean -- what you're saying makes more sense, obviously.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I mean, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I can't blame Mr. Ackerman for it either.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, quite honestly, Your Honour, he knew that we were going to produce this as an exhibit. But anyhow, let's try and keep one exhibit number now that we're -- the same one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I would suggest you do.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thanks, Mr. Filipovic. We'll see you again tomorrow at the same time, 2.15. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
